title: Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Mazdoor hit: three interests, one idea
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The interest of the nation, the industry and the worker must be protected together.
body:
Dattopant Thengadi gave BMS a holistic philosophy in three words: **Rashtra hita, Udyoga hita, Mazdoor hita**. In English, it is the interest of the nation, of the industry and of the worker. The formula appears under the BMS name on the organisation's website and is repeated in its meetings and publications. It is easy to say and harder to apply, and this post looks at what it means, why the order matters, and how it shows up in BMS's positions on real questions.

## The idea in brief

Most trade union traditions start from the worker's interest and treat the employer's interest as opposed to it. BMS starts from a wider frame. Its history, *The Onward March of BMS*, says that the organisation aimed at securing workers' interests within national interests, and that it regards society as a "third" and more important party in industrial relations, alongside the employer and the worker. The three-word formula is the short form of that thought.

It sits beside the three-line motto discussed earlier in this series, which speaks of nationalising the labour, labourising the industry and industrialising the nation. The motto describes a cycle; the formula names the three interests that the cycle must serve.

## The order matters

BMS places the **nation first**, then the **industry**, then the **worker**. This does not mean that the worker comes last in importance. It means that the worker's welfare is pursued within a framework where the nation and the industry also prosper. BMS's reasoning is that a strike which damages national interest, or a wage claim that destroys an industry, ends up hurting the worker too, since the worker's job depends on the industry's survival.

BMS also says that it is not driven by hostility to any class. Its website describes its fight as being against injustice and exploitation, not against any class, and says it is non-political and not linked to any party. The same page criticises other central trade union organisations for what it sees as their ties to political parties. These are BMS's own statements about its identity, and other organisations would describe themselves differently.

## Not a compromise

It would be wrong to read the formula as a way of asking workers to wait. BMS has pressed for minimum wages, social security and the recognition of scheme workers, as its pre-budget submissions show. In January 2025, for instance, it asked for the notification of the wages and social security codes, for a minimum EPS-95 pension of Rs 5,000 as a first step, and for scheme workers to be recognised as workers. Its position is that the three interests are **not opposed** to each other. A worker who is paid fairly produces better. An industry that treats its workers well becomes stronger. A strong industry builds the nation.

The economic ideas in BMS's history show that the formula can be demanding. *The Onward March of BMS* mentions proposals such as a ratio of 1:10 between minimum and maximum incomes, a ceiling on incomes, a right to work and a ban on luxury-goods industries. Whatever one thinks of these, they are not the proposals of an organisation that simply asks workers to be patient.

## Duty and right together

A distinctive feature of BMS's approach is that it pairs rights with duties. Its website says it supports workers' participation in industry tied to duties, and it advocates producing the maximum while consuming with restraint. One of its slogans says that workers will work in the country's interest and take full wages for the work. The two halves go together: a claim to a fair share, and a commitment to good work.

## In practice

You can see this idea in how BMS approaches policy questions.

- **Labour Codes.** In its pre-budget submission of January 2025, BMS asked that the Code on Wages and the Code on Social Security be notified, and that what it considers anti-worker provisions in the other two codes be removed. Supporting parts of a reform while objecting to others is the formula at work: it welcomes what serves workers and the wider economy and resists what it sees as harmful.
- **Public sector.** The Organiser's 2025 article on BMS says it opposes the privatisation of public sector undertakings while supporting ethical private employers. In its budget letter, BMS asked for a high-power committee, including unions, to plan the revival of sick public sector units, which reflects concern for both the industry and its workers.
- **Swadeshi and small industry.** BMS speaks for Swadeshi and for micro and small industries because they create jobs. In its budget letter it asked that rural micro and small industries be given priority under the Production Linked Incentive scheme and cheaper credit. Its website also records opposition to the New Economic Policy and to conditions attached to loans from the IMF and the World Bank.
- **Consultation.** BMS asks for tripartite consultation through the Indian Labour Conference and sits on bodies such as the Standing Labour Committee, the EPF and ESI bodies and the National Productivity Council. At the International Labour Conference it leads the Indian workers' delegation.
- **Method.** Strikes are a last resort after talks, negotiation and arbitration, and violence is opposed. A 2025 *Organiser* article, which is close to the movement, summarises the approach as nationalism, respect for labour and dialogue, and as solving problems through struggle and dialogue.

## How critics see it

Fairness requires noting the other side. Critics from other labour traditions say that putting the nation and industry before the worker can, in practice, ask workers to accept employer-friendly outcomes in the name of national interest, and that conflict between employers and workers is real and cannot be wished away. BMS answers that it does not shrink from struggle and that its record, from the 1963 Bombay Bundh to the 1974 railway strike, includes major agitations. The reader is left to judge by the facts of particular disputes, which is the best test for any philosophy.

## A reminder on the website

The three words also appear on this website, under the BMS name, as a reminder of the idea that guides it. A visitor reading the site will find the Hindi form, *Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Shramik hit*, on the organisation's At a Glance page together with the motto. For a new karyakarta, it is worth learning both the words and the reasoning, because the formula is a way of asking, in any dispute, who else besides the two parties at the table has a stake in the result.

## What remains to be done

The formula sets a high standard, and the test lies in cases where the interests seem to pull apart: a plant that is losing money, a reform that raises productivity but reduces job security, a scheme that delivers public services through workers who are not treated as workers. Later posts will look at some of these cases, including the Labour Codes and the position of scheme workers, and will ask how the three interests can be reconciled in each.
